metadata.title: Teachers’ engaging messages, students’ motivation to learn and academic performance: The moderating role of emotional intensity in speech

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a small, non-national sample of 36 teachers and 807 students from 16 secondary schools in Spain (Gran Canaria, Tenerife, and Santander). The analysis is based on observational audio recordings of teachers’ lessons and student motivation questionnaires plus school-record math grades; the manuscript does not report the use of TALIS/PISA-style sampling weights or any complex survey design adjustments. Because the models are estimated in MPlus using counterfactual mediation with moderation (and not via ILSA microdata PV scaling), there is no documented weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) to apply. Consequently, results should be interpreted as context-specific to the participating Spanish schools rather than population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variable is students’ math grades from Spanish official school records (0–10) rather than an ILSA cognitive achievement scale generated with PVs. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure for the analytic variables (e.g., questionnaire items, coded message categories, or grade records), so the missing-data strategy cannot be verified from the provided text. This is a reporting gap for transparency about how incomplete observations were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 36 secondary-school teachers (19 females, 17 males) and 807 students (Grades 9–12; mean age 16.39) from 16 secondary schools in Spain (Gran Canaria, Tenerife, and Santander). Teachers could participate with one or more groups, yielding 56 participant groups. Teachers audio-recorded eight lessons at the end of the first term; transcripts were AI-transcribed, filtered by a Python keyword script (retaining ~10% of the transcript), and then manually coded by two research assistants into engaging-message categories. For statistical analyses, message categories were restricted to those with sufficient observations: only nine of the sixteen frame/appeal categories were used (gain-framed extrinsic-normal; gain-framed extrinsic-achievement; gain-framed introjected-normal; gain-framed identified-normal; gain-framed identified-achievement; loss-framed extrinsic-achievement; loss-framed introjected-normal; loss-framed identified-normal; loss-framed identified-achievement). Emotional intensity was computed per message clip using the Emotional Temperature model and then averaged per teacher within each group; motivation to learn was measured in the second term via a Spanish 20-item scale (subscales for extrinsic, introjected, identified, intrinsic) administered via Google Forms; academic performance was the second-term math grade from official school records.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study is not an ILSA-based machine-learning paper: it uses transcript-based lesson analysis (TBLA) and acoustic scoring to examine how teachers’ engaging messages relate to students’ motivation to learn and subsequent math grades. The sample comprises 36 Spanish secondary teachers and 807 students (Grades 9–12) from 16 schools in Gran Canaria, Tenerife, and Santander. Teachers’ engaging messages were coded into gain/loss frames and motivational appeal types; emotional intensity was computed from audio clips using the Emotional Temperature model (0–100) and averaged per teacher-group. The authors estimated moderated mediation models in MPlus with a counterfactual mediation approach, segmenting emotional intensity into 10-point bins. Results show significant direct and total effects of engaging messages on academic performance for most message types, with emotional intensity often showing an inverse (diminishing) effect on performance; however, indirect effects through motivation to learn were not significant. Limitations include the small, localized sample and the absence of reported missing-data handling and any survey-weighting strategy. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the manuscript does not train or evaluate any machine-learning predictive model (no RF/XGBoost/SVM/NN, no ML validation metrics). Instead, it applies counterfactual mediation with moderation (a statistical modeling framework) to observational classroom and questionnaire data. Therefore, fields such as ml_techniques, plausible-values handling, and ILSA-specific PV/weight procedures are not applicable or not reported in the ML sense.
